units.t: Brand Stories. Episode one.
In this episode: Ford, Toyota and the art of making things, McDonald's and the franchise formula, Tupperware, Brownie Wise and the home party and The Post-it Note: a failed glue and a choir bookmark.
Part one. Ford, Toyota and the art of making things.
Two car companies, half a world apart, changed how almost everything is made, from your phone to your runners.
Their ideas still shape factories, hospitals and offices today.
Ford's moving assembly line.
In the early 1900s cars were hand-built toys for the wealthy.
Henry Ford wanted one ordinary families could afford.
His 1908 Model T was simple and tough, but making it cheap meant building it faster than anyone had.
His engineers broke the work into small, repeatable tasks, borrowing the overhead lines of Chicago meatpacking plants, where carcasses moved past workers who each made one cut.
Ford reversed the idea: instead of taking something apart, put a car together.
In 1913 Ford's Highland Park plant in Michigan introduced a moving assembly line.
The car travelled past workers who each repeated one task.
Assembly time for a Model T chassis fell from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half.
Prices fell, and by the 1920s millions were on the road, for years only in black.
The five dollar day.
The line had a human cost.
The work was monotonous and exhausting, and many workers quit soon after starting, so Ford was constantly hiring and training new people.
In 1914 the company announced five dollars a day for many workers, roughly double the typical factory wage, along with a shorter working day.
Crowds of job seekers gathered outside the factory.
The policy came with conditions, and the company inspected aspects of some workers' private lives.
Still, it cut turnover sharply and helped create a workforce that could afford the very cars it was building.
Mass production had arrived, and factories around the world rushed to copy it.
Toyota's different problem.
After World War II, Toyota faced the opposite situation to Ford.
Japan was recovering from devastation, money was scarce, and the market wanted many types of vehicle in modest numbers.
Huge runs of identical cars, backed by enormous stockpiles of parts, did not fit.
Engineers led by Taiichi Ohno developed the Toyota Production System, aiming to eliminate waste of every kind: overproduction, waiting, unnecessary movement, defects and excess inventory.
Ohno later said he drew inspiration from American supermarkets, which restock shelves only as customers take items away.
The result was just in time.
Each step pulls parts from the step before only when it needs them, often signalled by simple cards called kanban.
This keeps stockpiles small and exposes problems quickly.
Stop the line.
Toyota's second idea is jidoka, or automation with a human touch.
Machines stop when something goes wrong, and workers can pull a cord, called an andon, to halt the line when they spot a defect.
To outsiders this seemed crazy, because stopping a production line is expensive.
But fixing the cause immediately prevents thousands of faulty cars being built later.
Toyota also encouraged kaizen, or continuous improvement.
Workers on the factory floor were expected to suggest ways to make their own jobs safer, simpler and less wasteful.
One well-known technique is the 'five whys': ask why something happened, then ask why again about each answer, until you reach the root cause rather than the surface symptom.
Lean's reach and limits.
By the 1980s Toyota's cars had a strong reputation for reliability, and Western carmakers studied its methods closely.
A 1990 book, The Machine That Changed the World, helped spread the label 'lean production'.
Lean ideas now run through hospitals, software companies, warehouses and government offices.
Agile software teams, for example, borrow its small batches and quick feedback.
But lean has limits.
Holding little inventory works when supply chains run smoothly and fails when they break.
After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and again during COVID-19, shortages of parts such as computer chips halted car production around the world.
Many companies now hold larger buffers of critical components.
The deeper lesson is that how work is organised can matter as much as the technology.
The key idea: Ford's moving assembly line cut Model T build time from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half.
Part two. McDonald's and the franchise formula.
Two brothers built a fast, simple burger stand in California.
A milkshake machine salesman turned it into a global empire.
The secret was not really the burgers.
Speedee and Ray Kroc.
In 1940 brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald opened a drive-in in San Bernardino, California.
Frustrated by slow service, a long menu and the cost of carhops, they closed in 1948 and reopened with a radical idea.
The menu shrank to a handful of items, including hamburgers, cheeseburgers, fries, drinks and shakes.
Customers ordered at a window, and each worker had one task, almost like an assembly line.
Food was ready in moments.
They called it the Speedee Service System.
In 1954 Ray Kroc, a travelling salesman of Multimixer milkshake machines, visited after the restaurant ordered several.
He was amazed by the speed and the queues.
In 1955, in his fifties, he opened his own McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois, as the brothers' franchising agent.
How franchising works.
Franchising grows a business using other people's money and energy.
The franchisor owns the brand, the recipes and the operating system.
The franchisee, usually a local business owner, pays an upfront fee and ongoing payments, often a share of sales, for the right to run an outlet under that brand.
In return they get a recognised name, training, marketing and a tested way of doing things.
The idea was not new.
In the 1800s the Singer sewing machine company used licensed agents to sell its machines widely, and Coca-Cola licensed independent bottlers.
But McDonald's turned franchising into something close to a science, with detailed rules for almost everything.
Really a property business.
Kroc's early franchise deals earned only a small share of sales, and money was tight.
His financial adviser, Harry Sonneborn, came up with an influential idea.
The company would buy or lease the land for new restaurants, then rent it to franchisees, often with rent linked to sales.
This gave McDonald's a reliable income and considerable control, because a franchisee who broke the rules could lose the site.
Sonneborn is often credited with suggesting that the company was really in the real estate business rather than the hamburger business.
Property remains a major part of McDonald's finances.
Kroc grew increasingly frustrated with the brothers' cautious approach, and in 1961 he bought them out for $2.
7 million, a deal that later caused lasting bitterness.
The same burger everywhere.
Consistency became McDonald's great promise: a cheeseburger should taste the same in Chicago, Tokyo or Melbourne.
The company developed detailed manuals covering cooking times, portion sizes, cleaning and service.
In 1961 it opened a training school, Hamburger University, to teach managers and franchisees the system.
Suppliers had to meet exact specifications for beef, potatoes and buns.
Travellers knew precisely what they would get.
In 1986 The Economist even created the Big Mac Index, using the price of a Big Mac in different countries as a light-hearted way to compare currencies.
Australia's first McDonald's opened in Yagoona, in western Sydney, in December 1971.
Australians nicknamed the brand 'Maccas', and the company eventually embraced the name itself.
The franchise trade-off.
Many familiar Australian names in food, fitness, cleaning, real estate and retail run on a franchise model, giving many people a path to running their own business.
Buying into a well-known system can reduce some of the risks of starting from scratch, but it is not a guaranteed path to success.
Franchisees usually have little control over prices, menus or marketing, must pay ongoing fees even in lean times, and may be required to fund expensive renovations.
Some Australian franchise systems have faced disputes over profitability and scandals involving underpaid staff.
The Franchising Code of Conduct requires disclosure before signing.
This is general information, not legal or financial advice.
The ACCC website has a free guide for anyone considering buying a franchise.
The key idea: The McDonald brothers built a factory-style kitchen, and Ray Kroc saw it could be copied nationwide.
Part three. Tupperware, Brownie Wise and the home party.
A clever plastic container was gathering dust on shop shelves.
Then a single mother from Detroit worked out how to sell it, and changed direct selling for good.
Great product, poor sales.
Earl Tupper, an American inventor from New Hampshire, worked for DuPont in the late 1930s and became interested in polyethylene, a new plastic.
He developed ways to purify and mould it into containers that were light, unbreakable and flexible, unlike the brittle plastics of the time.
His real breakthrough was the lid.
Inspired by paint tin lids, he designed a seal that snapped on and could be made airtight by pressing out a little air, the famous burp.
Tupperware went on sale after the Second World War.
But in hardware and department stores it sat on shelves.
Plastic was a novelty, and the seal was not obvious from a container on a shelf.
Many people could not work out how to close the lids.
The product needed to be shown.
Enter Brownie Wise.
Some saleswomen working for home-selling companies such as Stanley Home Products had begun demonstrating Tupperware at gatherings in people's homes, with far better results than shops.
One was Brownie Wise.
Born in Georgia, she was a divorced single mother raising her son in Detroit.
She found Tupperware sold brilliantly when women could see it, touch it and watch the lid seal.
Wise built a network of dealers and moved to Florida, and her group's results caught Tupper's attention.
In 1951 he pulled Tupperware out of shops altogether and committed to home parties.
He put Wise in charge of the new sales operation, Tupperware Home Parties, with the title of vice-president.
How a party works.
The home party model was simple but powerful.
A host invited friends and neighbours to her house.
A dealer demonstrated the products, often with games and a playful show of how the seal kept food fresh or how a sealed bowl full of liquid could be tossed without spilling.
Guests could handle everything and place orders, and the host received a gift for organising it.
Buying from a friend in a relaxed social setting created a sense of trust and obligation that a shop counter could not match.
For many women in the 1950s, who were largely excluded from business careers, becoming a dealer offered independent income, flexible hours and the chance to rise through a sales organisation.
Recognition and a fall.
Wise understood motivation.
At the Florida headquarters she held lavish annual events, called jubilees, where top sellers won prizes ranging from appliances to cars and boats.
Recognition mattered as much as money.
Sales grew rapidly, and in 1954 Wise became the first woman on the cover of the American magazine Business Week.
But her fame and independence led to clashes with Tupper, who reportedly resented her growing profile.
In 1958 he dismissed her.
That same year he sold the company to the Rexall Drug Company for about sixteen million US dollars.
Wise received a modest payout, and for years her role was largely left out of the company's official history.
The party plan's legacy.
Tupperware became a global brand, and the party plan was copied by companies selling cosmetics, kitchenware, candles, jewellery and more.
It works because it combines demonstration with personal relationships, though critics note that social pressure to buy from a friend can be uncomfortable.
Times changed.
As more women worked outside the home and shopping moved online, the party model struggled, and Tupperware's sales declined for years.
In 2024 the company filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States.
Yet the core lesson remains sharp.
A product that customers do not understand will not sell, however good it is.
Finding the right way to show it can matter as much as inventing it.
The key idea: Tupperware's clever airtight seal sold poorly in shops because customers did not understand it.
Part four. The Post-it Note: a failed glue and a choir bookmark.
One of the world's best-known office products began as a glue that did not stick properly.
It took a scientist's persistence and a singer's frustration to see its value.
A glue that failed.
The company behind the Post-it Note turns setbacks into products.
It began in 1902 as the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company, set up to mine what the founders believed was valuable corundum.
The rock was poor quality, so the company moved into sandpaper, then masking tape and Scotch tape.
Since the late 1940s, technical staff have also been able to spend a share of their time, often described as fifteen per cent, on projects of their own choosing.
In 1968 3M chemist Spencer Silver tried to make a very strong adhesive and made an odd one instead.
It gripped lightly, so objects could be stuck down, peeled away and reused with little residue.
Silver was convinced it was special, but could not say what it was for.
A problem in the choir.
The breakthrough came from a colleague's annoyance.
Art Fry, a 3M product development engineer, sang in his church choir in Minnesota.
He marked hymns with scraps of paper, which kept falling out.
Around 1974 he remembered Spencer Silver's light adhesive and realised it could make the perfect bookmark: it would stay in place but peel off without tearing the page.
He began coating paper with the glue and experimenting.
Soon he noticed an even bigger use.
When he wrote a note on a sticky bookmark and stuck it on a report for a colleague, it worked as a message that stayed attached without damaging the document underneath.
A rocky launch.
Even with a working product, success was not guaranteed.
In 1977 3M test marketed the notes in four American cities as Press 'n Peel, and sales were disappointing.
Customers had never seen anything like it and could not imagine why they needed it.
Instead of giving up, the company changed tactics.
In 1978 it flooded Boise, Idaho, with free samples, an effort later nicknamed the Boise Blitz.
Once office workers actually used the notes, they wanted more, and a large majority of those surveyed said they would buy them.
Renamed Post-it Notes, the product launched across the United States in 1980 and in other countries soon after.
Today it is sold in well over a hundred countries.
Why the notes are yellow.
Many famous product features are carefully designed.
The colour of the Post-it Note was not.
According to the company's own telling, the team working on early versions used scrap paper that happened to be yellow, borrowed from a neighbouring laboratory.
The colour stuck, in more ways than one, and canary yellow became the signature.
It also proved practical, because a bright yellow square stands out on a desk, a computer screen or a page of black and white text.
Today the notes come in a rainbow of colours, sizes and shapes, but yellow remains the shade most people picture.
Not every successful choice in business comes from planning.
Lessons from a sticky note.
The Post-it story shows how innovation often really works.
It was not a single flash of genius.
It needed a technology nobody had a use for, a scientist stubborn enough to keep promoting it, a colleague with a real everyday problem, and a company culture that allowed time for side projects.
It also shows a marketing truth: a genuinely new product can fail if customers cannot picture using it, and letting people try it can be more persuasive than any advertisement.
Silver and Fry both received recognition for the invention, and Post-it Notes are now among the most recognisable office products ever made.
The key idea: Spencer Silver's weak, reusable adhesive looked like a failure but became the basis of the Post-it Note.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What made Ford's 1913 assembly line so much faster?
Answer. The car moved past workers who each repeated one task.
Question two. What was the key idea of the Speedee Service System?
Answer. A short menu and an assembly-line kitchen.
Question three. Why did Tupperware sell poorly in shops?
Answer. Shoppers could not see how the airtight seal worked.
Question four. Why did Spencer Silver's adhesive seem like a failure at first?
Answer. It gripped lightly, though it could be reused.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
